description: Build a personal CRM that holds 50 to 150 contacts organized into Dunbar tiers (5 intimate, 15 close, 50 regular, 150 acquaintance), tracks what matters about each person, sets a contact cadence per tier, and surfaces follow-ups when a contact falls past its cadence. The result is a system you can run from a spreadsheet or any contact tool, not a product you have to buy.

steps.description: Pull every meaningful contact out of scattered sources (phone, email, messaging apps, past calendars) into one roster, so the system starts from a complete picture instead of the handful of people who happen to be top of mind.

inputs.name: contact-sources
inputs.desc: The places your contacts currently live: phone contacts, email address book, messaging apps, social connections, past calendar invites, business cards

inputs.name: time-available
inputs.desc: How much time you can spend on the initial capture (a 30 minute pass captures the obvious people, a 2 hour pass catches the long tail)

outputs.name: raw-contact-roster
outputs.desc: A single de-duplicated list of every contact worth tracking, with name and at least one way to reach them

outputs.name: source-coverage-notes
outputs.desc: Which sources you pulled from and which you skipped, so you know where gaps remain

process: Export or copy contacts from each source into one list. Do not filter yet. A name you are unsure about stays in for now, because deleting is faster than remembering someone you dropped.
Remove duplicates by matching on email and phone first, then on name. When two records clearly belong to the same person, merge them and keep every reachable address.

Apply one inclusion test to each name: have you interacted with this person on purpose in the last two years, or do you expect to on purpose in the next one? If neither, move them to a separate parked list rather than the active roster.
Record which sources you covered. The long tail (old calendars, event attendee lists) holds people you have forgotten but who still matter, so note any source you did not have time to pull.

steps.description: Sort the roster into the four Dunbar tiers so that attention gets allocated by relationship closeness rather than by whoever contacted you most recently. The tier sizes are targets, not hard caps, but large overflows are a signal worth reading.

inputs.name: raw-contact-roster
inputs.desc: The de-duplicated list of contacts to tier

inputs.name: source-coverage-notes
inputs.desc: Where the roster came from and where gaps remain

outputs.name: tiered-roster
outputs.desc: Every contact assigned to one of four tiers: inner 5, close 15, regular 50, acquaintance 150

outputs.name: tier-overflow-flags
outputs.desc: Tiers that are far over their target size, with a note on what the overflow means

process: Assign the inner 5 first: the people you would call in a crisis at 2am. If you have more than 5, you are probably counting people you wish were that close rather than people who are. Keep it honest.

Assign the close 15 (minus the inner 5, so about 10 more): people you talk with regularly and would be genuinely sad to lose touch with. Then the regular 50: people you want ongoing contact with. Everyone else who passed the inclusion test lands in the acquaintance 150.
Place each person by actual closeness and by how much contact you want, not by how often they happen to reach you. A needy acquaintance who messages daily still belongs in the outer tier.

Flag any tier that is far over target. An inner 5 of 12 means the tier has lost its meaning. A regular 50 of 200 means you are trying to actively maintain more relationships than the research says is sustainable, and the cadence step will expose the strain.

steps.description: Define the small set of context fields the system will track for each contact, so that before any interaction you can recall what you last discussed, what matters to them, and what you promised. The field set is deliberately short so that keeping it current stays realistic.

inputs.name: tiered-roster
inputs.desc: Contacts sorted into Dunbar tiers

inputs.name: tier-overflow-flags
inputs.desc: Tiers over target size and what that signals

outputs.name: context-field-schema
outputs.desc: The fields tracked per contact: last contact date, what you last discussed, what matters to them, what you promised, next action

outputs.name: field-fill-priority
outputs.desc: Which fields to fill first by tier, so inner tiers get full context and outer tiers get the minimum

process: Define five fields and stop there. Last-contact-date, last-topic (one line on what you discussed), what-matters (what this person cares about or is working toward right now), open-promise (anything you said you would do), and next-action (the single next thing to do with them).

Set the rule that what-matters and open-promise are the two fields that actually change behavior, so they are mandatory for the inner 5 and close 15. For acquaintances, last-contact-date alone is enough to run the cadence.
Write a one-line example for each field so future entries stay consistent. Last-topic is not a transcript, it is a phrase like talked through their job search, not the whole conversation.

Decide the update trigger: fields get refreshed right after an interaction while it is fresh, not in a weekly batch, because the detail you want (what mattered to them that day) is gone by the weekend.

steps.description: Set a target contact cadence for each tier (inner 5 weekly, close 15 biweekly, regular 50 monthly, acquaintance 150 quarterly) and then pressure-test whether the total contact load those cadences imply is actually achievable in the time you have.

inputs.name: context-field-schema
inputs.desc: The per-contact fields including last contact date

inputs.name: field-fill-priority
inputs.desc: Which fields matter most per tier

outputs.name: tier-cadence-rules
outputs.desc: The target days between contacts for each tier, with any per-tier adjustments

outputs.name: cadence-load-estimate
outputs.desc: The number of touchpoints per week the cadences imply, checked against available time

process: Set the starting cadences: inner 5 weekly (7 days), close 15 biweekly (14 days), regular 50 monthly (30 days), acquaintance 150 quarterly (90 days). These are the defaults you will adjust.

Compute the implied weekly load. At full tier sizes this is roughly 5 weekly, 7.5 biweekly, 11.7 monthly, and 12.5 quarterly touchpoints, which lands near 36 contacts per week. Compare that to the time you actually have for relationship upkeep.

If the load exceeds your time, do not just miss cadences silently. Either lengthen the outer-tier cadences (acquaintances every 180 days instead of 90) or shrink the tiers. A cadence you cannot meet trains you to ignore the system.

Allow per-contact overrides for known rhythms. A friend you see every holiday does not need a monthly nudge, and a mentor you want to stay close to may warrant a tighter cadence than their tier default.

steps.description: Map the schema and cadence rules onto whatever tool will actually hold the data (a spreadsheet, a notes app, phone contact fields, or a dedicated contact tool), choosing the tool by whether you will keep it current rather than by its feature list.

inputs.name: tier-cadence-rules
inputs.desc: Target days between contacts per tier

inputs.name: cadence-load-estimate
inputs.desc: Implied weekly contact load versus available time

outputs.name: tool-field-mapping
outputs.desc: How each schema field maps to a column, property, or custom field in the chosen tool

outputs.name: automation-options
outputs.desc: Which parts can be computed automatically (next-due date) versus which stay manual in this tool

process: Pick the tool by one test: where will you reliably update a record 30 seconds after a conversation? A spreadsheet you keep open beats a polished tool you forget to open.

Map each field to a column or property. Add one computed field, next-due-date, as last-contact-date plus the cadence for that tier. In a spreadsheet this is a formula, in a contact app it may be a manual date you set.

Decide what the tool can automate. If it supports computed dates and filtered views, set next-due-date to recalculate automatically. If not, plan a weekly recalculation pass instead of pretending the tool will do it.

Keep the schema identical across whatever tools you use. If contacts live half in your phone and half in a sheet, the same five fields appear in both so a future consolidation is a copy, not a redesign.

steps.description: Turn the stored data into a working queue by surfacing exactly the contacts who have fallen past their tier cadence, sorted so the most overdue and most important rise to the top instead of drowning in the full list.

inputs.name: tool-field-mapping
inputs.desc: How fields map to the chosen tool, including the next-due date

inputs.name: automation-options
inputs.desc: What the tool computes automatically versus manually

outputs.name: overdue-followup-queue
outputs.desc: Contacts whose next-due date has passed, sorted by how overdue and by tier priority

outputs.name: cadence-breach-report
outputs.desc: A summary of how many contacts per tier are overdue, revealing where the cadence is systematically slipping

process: Build one view that filters to contacts where next-due-date is in the past. This is the only view you need day to day. Everything else is reporting.
Sort the queue by days-overdue within tier, so an inner-5 person two days late outranks an acquaintance a month late. Closeness breaks ties, not raw overdue days.

Produce the breach report: overdue count per tier. If the acquaintance tier is almost entirely overdue, the cadence is too aggressive for that tier and should be lengthened rather than endlessly chased.
Keep the queue small enough to act on. If it is always hundreds long, the cadences are unrealistic and the fix is in the cadence rules, not in trying harder to clear an impossible list.

steps.description: Install the lightweight weekly ritual that keeps the system alive: clear the overdue queue, log new interactions, and watch a few health metrics so that a stale CRM gets caught early instead of quietly dying.

inputs.name: overdue-followup-queue
inputs.desc: The sorted queue of contacts past cadence

inputs.name: cadence-breach-report
inputs.desc: Per-tier overdue counts

outputs.name: review-ritual-plan
outputs.desc: A fixed weekly routine (when, how long, what steps) for working the queue and updating records

outputs.name: maintenance-metrics
outputs.desc: The handful of numbers that tell you the system is healthy: percent of contacts within cadence, queue length trend, records updated this week

process: Set a fixed weekly slot of 20 to 30 minutes. A floating review that competes with everything else does not happen. Put it on the calendar as a recurring block.
Run the same three steps each week: work the top of the overdue queue (not the whole thing), log any interactions you have not yet recorded, and reset next-due dates for anyone you contacted.

Track three numbers only: percent of contacts currently within their cadence (the headline health metric), the trend in queue length (growing means the system is losing), and records updated this week (near zero means you have stopped using it).

Review the metrics monthly against the cadence rules. If a tier is chronically out of cadence despite effort, that is data: lengthen the cadence, shrink the tier, or accept that some outer-tier contacts are really parked, not active.

description: Track the emotional deposits and withdrawals in your most important relationships using Covey's emotional bank account model, so that before any withdrawal (a favor, a hard piece of news, a request) you can check the balance first. The same ledger works for personal relationships, manager and report relationships, client relationships, and vendor relationships, with only the deposit and withdrawal definitions shifting by context.

steps.description: Select the top 20 relationships to put on the ledger and tag each by context, because tracking every relationship is unsustainable and the value comes from attention to the relationships where a drained balance would cost you the most.

inputs.name: relationship-pool
inputs.desc: The full set of relationships you could track across work and personal life

inputs.name: relationship-context
inputs.desc: The contexts in play: personal, manager-and-report, client, vendor, or a mix

outputs.name: top-relationships
outputs.desc: The 20 relationships that go on the ledger, chosen by importance and by the cost of a drained balance

outputs.name: context-tags
outputs.desc: Each relationship tagged by context, since deposits and withdrawals mean different things in each

process: List candidate relationships and score each on two axes: how much you depend on it, and how damaging a low balance would be. A vendor you rarely need but who holds a single point of failure can still make the list.
Take the top 20. Fewer is fine. More than 20 and the ledger becomes a chore you abandon. The point is sustained attention to the few that carry real weight.
Tag each with its context (personal, manager, report, client, vendor). The context determines what counts as a deposit later, so do not skip it.
Note any relationship that spans two contexts (a colleague who is also a friend). These carry two ledgers that can diverge, and a withdrawal in one context can draw down the balance in the other.

steps.description: Define what actually counts as a deposit and a withdrawal in each context, because an abstract model is useless until you can name the concrete behaviors that build or spend trust with these specific people.

inputs.name: top-relationships
inputs.desc: The 20 relationships on the ledger

inputs.name: context-tags
inputs.desc: The context of each relationship

outputs.name: deposit-catalog
outputs.desc: The concrete deposit behaviors per context: keeping commitments, clarifying expectations, small kindnesses, loyalty in their absence, sincere apologies

outputs.name: withdrawal-catalog
outputs.desc: The concrete withdrawal behaviors per context: broken promises, unclear expectations, unkindness, criticism behind their back, requests and favors

process: Start from Covey's six deposit types (keeping commitments, clarifying expectations, attending to small things, showing personal integrity and loyalty to the absent, delivering sincere apologies when you withdraw, understanding the individual) and translate each into a concrete behavior for your contexts.

For deposits, write what it looks like with these people specifically. In a manager relationship, a deposit is defending your report in a meeting they are not in. In a client relationship, it is flagging a problem before they notice it.

For withdrawals, be honest about the ordinary ones. Asking for a favor is a withdrawal even when granted. Delivering bad news is a withdrawal even when necessary. A withdrawal is not a wrong, it is a draw on the balance.

Note the asymmetry: in most relationships a withdrawal spends more than a deposit builds, so trust is slow to accumulate and fast to drain. Your catalogs should reflect that a broken promise can undo many small kindnesses.

steps.description: Estimate the current balance in each relationship by reviewing recent deposits and withdrawals, producing a rough reading (healthy, thin, overdrawn) rather than a false-precision number, since the goal is to know which accounts are safe to draw on.

inputs.name: deposit-catalog
inputs.desc: Concrete deposit behaviors per context

inputs.name: withdrawal-catalog
inputs.desc: Concrete withdrawal behaviors per context

outputs.name: balance-estimates
outputs.desc: A rough balance reading per relationship: healthy, thin, or overdrawn, with the reasoning

outputs.name: recent-activity-log
outputs.desc: The recent deposits and withdrawals you recalled for each relationship, as the evidence behind the reading

process: For each relationship, recall the last several months of interactions and sort them into deposits and withdrawals using your catalogs. Write them down, because memory favors the dramatic and forgets the quiet deposits.

Read the balance qualitatively. Healthy means recent deposits clearly outweigh withdrawals and the relationship absorbs a mistake without strain. Thin means it is roughly even and a withdrawal would be felt. Overdrawn means recent withdrawals dominate and the relationship is running on goodwill you no longer have.
Weight recency and withdrawals more heavily. A deposit from a year ago counts for little, and a single serious withdrawal (a broken commitment) can overwhelm months of small deposits.
Resist false precision. A number like 73 implies a measurement you did not make. Three bands (healthy, thin, overdrawn) are enough to drive the decisions that follow.

steps.description: Identify the thin and overdrawn accounts and separate the ones that are low because of neglect from the ones that are low because of an unrepaired withdrawal, since the two call for different responses.

inputs.name: balance-estimates
inputs.desc: The qualitative balance reading per relationship

inputs.name: recent-activity-log
inputs.desc: The deposits and withdrawals behind each reading

outputs.name: low-account-list
outputs.desc: The thin and overdrawn relationships, ranked by a combination of how low and how important

outputs.name: overdrawn-warnings
outputs.desc: Relationships where the balance is low enough that any near-term withdrawal would cause real damage

process: Pull every relationship reading thin or overdrawn into one list. Rank by combining how low the balance is with how important the relationship is, so an overdrawn inner relationship outranks a thin peripheral one.

Diagnose the cause for each. Neglect-low means the balance faded from inattention (no recent deposits, no specific wrong). Withdrawal-low means a specific unrepaired withdrawal is dragging it down. The log tells you which.
Flag the overdrawn accounts as warnings. These are relationships where you cannot safely ask for anything right now, and attempting a withdrawal would push them toward rupture.
Note any relationship that is important and overdrawn at the same time. That combination is the highest risk on the ledger and gets first claim on your repair attention.

steps.description: Build specific deposit plans for the low accounts, matched to cause, because a neglect-low account recovers through steady small deposits while a withdrawal-low account recovers only through a sincere apology and changed behavior, not through unrelated niceness.

inputs.name: low-account-list
inputs.desc: Thin and overdrawn relationships ranked and diagnosed

inputs.name: overdrawn-warnings
inputs.desc: Accounts too low for any near-term withdrawal

outputs.name: deposit-plans
outputs.desc: Per-relationship deposit plans matched to cause, with specific actions drawn from the deposit catalog

outputs.name: deposit-schedule
outputs.desc: When each deposit happens, paced so the deposits read as genuine rather than as a sudden transactional campaign

process: For neglect-low accounts, plan a series of small genuine deposits over time: attend to the small things, follow through on a minor commitment, make contact with no ask attached. Consistency rebuilds these, not a grand gesture.

For withdrawal-low accounts, the first deposit is usually a sincere apology that names the specific withdrawal, without excuses, followed by visibly changed behavior. Unrelated kindness before the apology reads as avoidance and can deepen the deficit.

Draw each action from the deposit catalog so it fits the context. A client deposit (proactively flagging a risk) differs from a personal deposit (remembering what matters to them), and using the wrong register can feel hollow.

Pace the schedule so deposits do not arrive all at once. A sudden flood of attention right before you need something is itself read as a withdrawal, because the motive is obvious. Spread deposits so they look like how you treat the relationship, not like a down payment on a request.

steps.description: Create the pre-withdrawal check, the core payoff of the ledger: a short protocol you run before any favor, hard conversation, or request, so that you draw on healthy accounts and shore up thin ones before drawing rather than after causing damage.

inputs.name: deposit-plans
inputs.desc: The deposit plans for low accounts

inputs.name: deposit-schedule
inputs.desc: The timing of planned deposits

outputs.name: withdrawal-checklist
outputs.desc: The short checklist to run before any withdrawal: current balance, size of the withdrawal, whether to deposit first or proceed

outputs.name: withdrawal-timing-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for when to delay a withdrawal to build balance first and when the withdrawal cannot wait

process: Write the checklist as three questions: what is the current balance in this account, how large is the withdrawal I am about to make, and does the balance comfortably cover it?

Set the decision rule. Healthy balance and small withdrawal: proceed. Thin balance or large withdrawal: deposit first if you can, or at minimum acknowledge the draw (name that you are asking a lot). Overdrawn: do not withdraw unless it is unavoidable.

Add timing rules for the unavoidable case. Some withdrawals cannot wait (urgent bad news, a time-boxed request). When you must withdraw from a low account, pair it with an immediate sincere acknowledgment and a concrete plan to rebuild, so the draw does not read as careless.

Make the check a habit by attaching it to a trigger: before sending a request, before a performance conversation, before asking a vendor for an exception. The check is worthless if you only remember it after the relationship is already strained.

steps.description: Adapt the finished ledger to each relationship context so the same model runs correctly for personal, manager-and-report, client, and vendor relationships, and flag the cross-context cases where a withdrawal in one role draws down trust in another.

inputs.name: withdrawal-checklist
inputs.desc: The pre-withdrawal check

inputs.name: withdrawal-timing-rules
inputs.desc: When to delay a withdrawal versus proceed

outputs.name: context-adapted-ledgers
outputs.desc: The ledger tuned per context, with context-specific deposits, withdrawals, and power dynamics accounted for

outputs.name: cross-context-cautions
outputs.desc: Relationships spanning two contexts where a withdrawal in one role spends trust in the other

process: For manager-and-report relationships, account for power asymmetry. A withdrawal from a report (extra work, a hard review) costs more than the same ask between peers, because the report has less freedom to refuse, so the required balance is higher.

For client relationships, treat reliability and proactive communication as the heaviest deposits, and treat surprises (even good ones delivered badly) as withdrawals. Clients bank trust mostly through predictability.

For vendor relationships, remember the ledger runs both directions and often outlasts individuals. Deposits like paying on time and giving clear specifications build balance you will need when you ask for an exception later.

List the cross-context relationships and set a caution for each: a withdrawal you make as a manager can drain the balance you hold as a friend, and the person does not keep the two accounts as separate as you do. Decide in advance which role governs when they conflict.

description: Replace cold outreach (1 to 3 percent response) with warm introductions (40 to 60 percent response) by finding a mutual connection, crafting a blurb the connector can forward without editing, framing the introduction so it benefits both sides, tracking the chain, and following up with the connector whether or not the introduction converts. The follow-up is what keeps the connector willing to introduce you again.

steps.description: Define precisely who you want to reach and why, because a specific target (a named person or a tightly described role) makes mutual connections findable and makes the eventual ask easy for a connector to act on, while a vague target stalls the whole chain.

inputs.name: outreach-goal
inputs.desc: What you are trying to accomplish with the introduction (a sale, a hire, advice, a partnership, a job)

inputs.name: target-criteria
inputs.desc: The attributes of the right person to reach: role, company type, seniority, location, or a specific named individual

outputs.name: target-profile
outputs.desc: A precise description of the person or role to reach, specific enough that a connector could recognize who fits

outputs.name: target-shortlist
outputs.desc: Named individuals who fit the profile, where you can name them, in priority order

process: State the goal of the introduction in one sentence, because the goal determines who the right target is. Advice, a sale, and a job each point to different people even in the same company.

Turn the criteria into a profile a stranger could match against. Not someone in operations but a VP of operations at a mid-size logistics company dealing with route planning. Specificity is what lets a connector think of a name.
Where you can, name actual individuals who fit, and rank them. A named target makes the mutual-connection search concrete instead of hypothetical.
Sanity check that the target can actually give you what you want. The most senior person is often not the right target, because the person with the problem you solve may be two levels down.

steps.description: Find the people who sit between you and the target, mapping every path you can (shared employers, schools, communities, second-degree connections) so you are choosing from several possible connectors rather than forcing the one obvious path.

inputs.name: target-profile
inputs.desc: The precise description of who to reach

inputs.name: target-shortlist
inputs.desc: Named individuals who fit, in priority order

outputs.name: mutual-connection-map
outputs.desc: For each target, the mutual connections who could introduce you, including multi-hop paths

outputs.name: connection-strength-notes
outputs.desc: How strong each potential connector's relationship is with both you and the target

process: For each named target, list everyone you know who plausibly knows them: shared current or former employers, schools, professional communities, and people whose networks overlap with the target's world.

Include second-degree paths where a direct connection does not exist. A two-hop path (you know A, A knows the target) is still far warmer than cold, and sometimes A is more willing than a closer but busier connector.

For each potential connector, note the strength of their relationship with you and, separately, with the target. A connector who barely knows the target cannot make a warm introduction no matter how well they know you.
Do not filter yet. Map all the paths first. The selection step weighs them, and a path you dismiss early (an old colleague you have not spoken to in a while) sometimes turns out to be the strongest.

steps.description: Choose the best connector for each target by balancing relationship strength on both sides against how much social capital the ask will cost the connector, since the ideal connector knows the target well, thinks well of you, and will not be overspending their own credibility by introducing you.

inputs.name: mutual-connection-map
inputs.desc: Potential connectors and paths per target

inputs.name: connection-strength-notes
inputs.desc: Relationship strength on both sides

outputs.name: selected-connectors
outputs.desc: The chosen connector for each target, with a backup where one exists

outputs.name: connector-fit-rationale
outputs.desc: Why each connector was chosen, and the cost the introduction imposes on them

process: Score each potential connector on three things: strength of their tie to the target, how favorably they view you, and how low the cost of the ask is to them. The best connector is strong on all three, not just the first.

Prefer a connector for whom the introduction is a small deposit, not a large withdrawal. Someone who introduces people routinely and whose standing with the target is secure can make the introduction without risking their own credibility.
Avoid overusing one super-connector for every target. Spreading asks protects the relationship you most rely on and keeps any single person from feeling mined.
Pick a backup connector where the map allows, so that if the first connector declines or goes quiet, you are not restarting the search from zero.

steps.description: Write the forwardable blurb, the single most important artifact in the chain: a short self-contained paragraph the connector can forward to the target with one line of their own, so making the introduction costs them 30 seconds instead of real effort.

inputs.name: selected-connectors
inputs.desc: The chosen connector per target

inputs.name: connector-fit-rationale
inputs.desc: Why each connector fits and the cost to them

outputs.name: forwardable-blurb
outputs.desc: A short paragraph the connector can forward as-is: who you are, why you are reaching out to this target, and what you are asking for

outputs.name: blurb-variants
outputs.desc: Versions tuned to the ask (advice, sale, hire) and to the target's likely priorities

process: Write the blurb so the connector does zero work. It should say who you are in one line, why this specific target (not a generic pitch), and the single clear ask, short enough to forward from a phone.
Make the ask small and concrete. A 20 minute call about a specific topic converts far better than an open-ended request to connect, because the target can gauge the cost immediately.
Lead with something the target will recognize as relevant to them, not with your credentials. The target reads the forward asking why should I care, and the first sentence has to answer that.
Write variants for the different ask types and target priorities, so the connector can pick the one that fits, and so you are not sending a sales-shaped blurb when the ask is really for advice.

steps.description: Frame the introduction as a benefit to both the target and the connector, not just to you, and build in the reputation protection that makes a connector comfortable, since the biggest reason introductions do not happen is the connector's fear of looking bad if it goes poorly.

inputs.name: forwardable-blurb
inputs.desc: The self-contained blurb to forward

inputs.name: blurb-variants
inputs.desc: Versions tuned to ask type and target priorities

outputs.name: mutual-benefit-statement
outputs.desc: A clear statement of what the target gains and what the connector gains from making the introduction

outputs.name: referrer-risk-reducers
outputs.desc: The elements that lower the connector's reputation risk: a low-commitment first step, an easy out, and no pressure on the target

process: Name what the target gains. If you cannot articulate why the introduction is good for them independent of what you want, the introduction is a favor, not a match, and it will convert poorly and strain the connector.
Name what the connector gains. Often it is social capital (they look connected and helpful) or the satisfaction of a good match. Make it easy for them to feel good about forwarding it.

Reduce the connector's risk directly. Offer the target a low-commitment first step (a short call, no obligation) and an explicit easy out, so that if the target is not interested, the connector has not spent credibility pushing something unwanted.

Remove pressure from the ask. The connector should be able to forward the blurb and step back, not feel they must advocate or chase. Low-pressure introductions preserve the connector's willingness to introduce you again.

steps.description: Track every introduction through its stages (asked, forwarded, target responded, meeting held, outcome) so that nothing stalls silently, you know when to nudge gently, and you can later see which connectors and framings actually produce results.

inputs.name: mutual-benefit-statement
inputs.desc: What target and connector each gain

inputs.name: referrer-risk-reducers
inputs.desc: The reputation-risk reducers built into the ask

outputs.name: intro-tracking-log
outputs.desc: A log of each introduction: target, connector, date asked, current stage, and outcome

outputs.name: intro-status-states
outputs.desc: The defined stages an introduction moves through and the action due at each

process: Define the stages: asked the connector, connector forwarded, target responded, meeting held, outcome reached. Each introduction sits in exactly one stage so you always know what is next.
Log every introduction against these stages with dates. The dates tell you when something has stalled (a connector who has not forwarded after a week, a target who has not replied after two).

Set the action due at each stage. After asking, the ball is with the connector, so wait. After forwarding with no target response, a single gentle nudge to the connector is appropriate, never repeated pressure.

Record outcomes even for the ones that die, because the pattern across many introductions is what later tells you which connectors convert and which framings land, and which targets were never a real fit.

steps.description: Close the loop with every connector regardless of outcome, because the follow-up is what sustains the introduction engine: a connector who is thanked and told what happened will introduce you again, while one who hears nothing back quietly stops.

inputs.name: intro-tracking-log
inputs.desc: The log of introductions and their stages

inputs.name: intro-status-states
inputs.desc: The stages and the action due at each

outputs.name: connector-followup-plan
outputs.desc: A plan for closing the loop with each connector: thank them, report what happened, and offer reciprocation

outputs.name: connector-acknowledgment-notes
outputs.desc: Notes on how each connector prefers to be acknowledged and what you owe them in return

process: Thank the connector within a day of the introduction being forwarded, before any outcome is known. This acknowledges the act of introducing, which is the part they controlled, and it is the most important touch.

Close the loop at the outcome. If it converted, share the good result and credit them. If it did not, thank them anyway and say briefly that it was not a fit, without blaming their contact. Both outcomes earn a report.

Look for a way to reciprocate. The durable introduction engine runs on two-way value, so note what the connector cares about and make an introduction for them, or help in some other way, so the ledger stays balanced.

Record how each connector likes to be acknowledged (a quick note, a public thank-you with permission, a returned favor) so future follow-ups fit them, and so a reliable connector feels valued rather than used.

description: Find the relationships that mattered but have been neglected, before they atrophy past recovery. List the people who were important two years ago, date your last real contact with each, decide which are worth recovering, and reach out with something specific rather than a hollow checking in. Unresolved relationship debt (the people you keep meaning to contact) drains background energy without ever producing action, so the audit either clears the debt or consciously releases it.

steps.description: Rebuild the list of people who genuinely mattered roughly two years ago, using memory prompts to surface the ones you have forgotten, because the relationships quietly draining you are usually the ones you cannot casually recall.

inputs.name: memory-prompts
inputs.desc: Sources that jog memory of past-important people: old calendars, photos, past projects, previous jobs, old message threads

inputs.name: lookback-window
inputs.desc: How far back to look (two years is the default, long enough that neglect shows but short enough that recovery is realistic)

outputs.name: past-important-list
outputs.desc: People who clearly mattered within the lookback window: close colleagues, friends, mentors, collaborators

outputs.name: recall-confidence-notes
outputs.desc: How vividly you remember each relationship, since faint recall is itself a signal of how far the relationship has decayed

process: Work through memory prompts rather than freelancing from memory. Open old calendars, past project rosters, photos, and message threads from around the lookback window. The point is to surface people who have fallen off your mental map.
Aim for around 30 people. Include anyone who was a real part of your life or work then: close colleagues, friends, mentors, people you collaborated with closely.

For each, note how vividly you recall them. A person you have to reconstruct from a calendar entry is further gone than one whose face comes immediately, and that gap predicts how hard recovery will be.
Do not pre-judge who is worth keeping yet. This step is pure recall. Filtering now would drop exactly the neglected relationships the audit exists to catch.

steps.description: Date your last real interaction with each person (a genuine exchange, not a passive like or a mass message) and rank by silence duration, so the extent of each relationship's decay becomes a concrete number instead of a vague sense of having been out of touch.

inputs.name: past-important-list
inputs.desc: The people who mattered within the lookback window

inputs.name: recall-confidence-notes
inputs.desc: How vividly each relationship is remembered

outputs.name: last-contact-dates
outputs.desc: The date of the last genuine two-way interaction with each person

outputs.name: silence-duration-ranking
outputs.desc: The list ranked by how long the silence has run, from most recently in touch to most decayed

process: For each person, find the last real interaction: a conversation, a genuine message exchange, a meeting. Do not count passive signals like seeing their post or a group broadcast. Those feel like contact but are not.
Where you cannot find an exact date, estimate to the season (spring two years ago). An approximate date is enough to rank, and chasing precision here wastes the audit's time.

Rank by silence duration. The ranking matters because recently dormant relationships are easy to restart while the longest-silent ones may not remember you well, which changes the reconnection approach.

Notice where silence duration and recall confidence disagree. A person you remember vividly but have not contacted in two years is a relationship you have been carrying as debt, meaning to reach out and never doing it.

steps.description: Decide which dormant relationships are actually worth recovering, scoring each on genuine mutual value and realistic recoverability, so effort goes to relationships that can and should come back rather than to every name on the list out of guilt.

inputs.name: last-contact-dates
inputs.desc: The last genuine contact date per person

inputs.name: silence-duration-ranking
inputs.desc: The list ranked by length of silence

outputs.name: recovery-worth-scores
outputs.desc: Each relationship scored on mutual value and on how realistically it can be recovered

outputs.name: recovery-candidates
outputs.desc: The subset worth actively recovering, separated from those to let rest

process: Score each relationship on value: what did it bring when it was active (meaning, growth, collaboration, support), and is that value still relevant to who you are now? Some relationships were tied to a job or a phase that has passed.

Score each on recoverability: how warm was the ending, how long the silence, and whether there is a natural reason to reconnect. A relationship that ended warmly and recently is highly recoverable, one that drifted after a falling-out is not.

Separate the genuinely worth-recovering from the guilt-driven. You are allowed to decide a relationship ran its course. Keeping a dead relationship on the active list is itself the debt the audit is trying to clear.
Produce the candidate list, deliberately short. Reconnecting well with five people beats sending ten hollow messages, because each real reconnection takes a specific, thoughtful approach.

steps.description: Identify the unresolved open loops behind the relationships (an unanswered message, an unkept promise, an unspoken apology) because that specific open loop is what turns a dormant relationship into background energy drain, and naming it is the first step to closing it.

inputs.name: recovery-worth-scores
inputs.desc: Value and recoverability scores per relationship

inputs.name: recovery-candidates
inputs.desc: The relationships worth actively recovering

outputs.name: open-loop-list
outputs.desc: The specific unresolved thread behind each neglected relationship, where one exists

outputs.name: energy-drain-flags
outputs.desc: Relationships that carry real background energy cost, whether or not you choose to recover them

process: For each candidate, ask what is actually unresolved. Often there is a specific open loop: a message you never answered, a promise you did not keep, a thank-you you never sent, a conversation that ended badly.
Recognize that the open loop, not the mere passage of time, is usually what makes a dormant relationship weigh on you. You avoid reaching out because reaching out means facing the unanswered thing.

Flag the relationships that carry genuine energy cost. These are the ones that surface in your mind unprompted, the ones you keep meaning to deal with. That recurring background thought is the debt made visible.

Note that some drains attach to relationships you decided not to recover. Those still need closing, because an unresolved loop drains energy even when you do not want the relationship back, which the closure step handles.

steps.description: Draft reconnection messages built around something specific to each person (a shared memory, a reason they came to mind, a genuine update) rather than a generic checking in, because specificity is what signals the relationship mattered and what makes a reply likely.

inputs.name: open-loop-list
inputs.desc: The unresolved thread behind each relationship

inputs.name: energy-drain-flags
inputs.desc: Relationships carrying real background energy cost

outputs.name: reconnect-drafts
outputs.desc: A specific, personal reconnection message for each recovery candidate

outputs.name: reconnect-hooks
outputs.desc: The concrete hook each message hangs on: a shared memory, a relevant update, a reason they came to mind, an overdue acknowledgment

process: For each candidate, find the hook: a specific shared memory, a piece of news relevant to them, an honest reason they came to mind, or the overdue acknowledgment the open loop calls for. The hook is the message.
Where there is an open loop, address it directly and simply. A brief honest line (I owed you a reply and I am sorry it is two years late) clears far more than pretending the gap did not happen.

Keep the message low-pressure. Reconnection after long silence works when it asks for nothing beyond the exchange itself, because a reconnect that leads with a request reads as reaching out only because you need something.

Write each message to one person. A reconnection that could have been sent to anyone signals the opposite of what you intend, and the whole point is to show this specific relationship was worth remembering.

steps.description: Decide, for every relationship on the audit, whether to recover it or release it, and log the decision, so the audit ends with a cleared ledger: active reconnection for the ones worth it, conscious closure for the rest, and no lingering open loops silently draining energy.

inputs.name: reconnect-drafts
inputs.desc: The specific reconnection messages

inputs.name: reconnect-hooks
inputs.desc: The concrete hook behind each message

outputs.name: recover-or-release-decisions
outputs.desc: For each relationship: recover (send the reconnect) or release (consciously let it rest), with the reasoning

outputs.name: debt-clearance-log
outputs.desc: A record of what was sent, what was released, and which open loops were closed, so the audit has a clean endpoint

process: Make an explicit recover-or-release call for every name, including the ones you are not reconnecting with. Leaving a name undecided is how it drifts back onto the mental list and resumes draining energy.

For recover decisions, send the reconnection message rather than letting it sit as a perfect unsent draft. An imperfect message sent today beats a polished one that never goes out, which is how the debt accumulated in the first place.

For release decisions, close any open loop first where it is owed. Even when you are letting a relationship rest, sending the overdue apology or acknowledgment closes the loop so it stops surfacing in your mind.
Log every outcome: sent, released, loop closed. The log is the point. An audit that ends with a clear record of what you did is a cleared debt, and you can re-run it in a year against a clean slate.

description: Map the flow of value in your network: for each key relationship, what you give, what they give, and whether the exchange is balanced. Imbalanced relationships are unstable (chronic over-givers burn out, chronic under-givers get quietly dropped), so the map identifies where you over-give and where you under-give and produces a plan to rebalance before the instability forces the issue.

steps.description: Select the relationships to map and define the value lens you will measure through, because reciprocity means different things in different relationships and a single money-only lens would misread a friendship that trades mostly in support and attention.

inputs.name: network-list
inputs.desc: The relationships you could map across personal and professional life

inputs.name: value-lens
inputs.desc: The kinds of value that count: time, help, money, introductions, emotional support, information, opportunities

outputs.name: focus-relationships
outputs.desc: The relationships to map, chosen where the exchange is significant enough that imbalance would matter

outputs.name: lens-definition
outputs.desc: The explicit definition of what counts as value in these relationships, so give and receive are measured consistently

process: Choose relationships where enough value flows that balance matters. A relationship with almost no exchange cannot be meaningfully imbalanced, so focus on the ones carrying real give and take.

Define the value lens explicitly and broadly. Value is not just favors or money, it includes time, attention, emotional support, information, introductions, and opportunities. A narrow lens makes healthy relationships look one-sided.

Match the lens to the relationship type. In a friendship, emotional support and presence dominate. In a professional relationship, information, introductions, and opportunities weigh more. Use the right lens for each.
Keep the set manageable, around 10 to 20 relationships. Mapping value flow honestly takes thought per relationship, and a bloated list gets filled in carelessly.

steps.description: Inventory what you give to each relationship across the full value lens, honestly and concretely, since most people either undercount their giving (and feel resentful) or overcount it (and feel entitled), and the rebalance depends on an accurate count.

inputs.name: focus-relationships
inputs.desc: The relationships being mapped

inputs.name: lens-definition
inputs.desc: What counts as value in these relationships

outputs.name: give-inventory
outputs.desc: For each relationship, the concrete things you give across the value lens

outputs.name: give-frequency-notes
outputs.desc: How often and how substantially you give, so a one-time large gift is not confused with steady small support

process: For each relationship, list what you actually give across every category in the lens: time spent, help offered, support provided, information shared, introductions made, opportunities passed along.
Be concrete, not aspirational. Count what you have genuinely given recently, not what you intend to give or what you gave once years ago. The map needs current reality.

Record frequency and weight, because they change the picture. Steady small support reads very differently from a single large favor, and both differ from availability (being reliably there) which is a real but easily overlooked form of giving.
Watch your own bias. If you tend toward resentment, you likely undercount. If you tend toward entitlement, you likely overcount. Name your lean and correct for it deliberately.

steps.description: Inventory what each person gives you across the same value lens, which is harder to see clearly because received value (especially emotional support, information, and access) is easy to take for granted and to undercount.

inputs.name: give-inventory
inputs.desc: What you give to each relationship

inputs.name: give-frequency-notes
inputs.desc: Frequency and weight of your giving

outputs.name: receive-inventory
outputs.desc: For each relationship, the concrete things they give you across the value lens

outputs.name: receive-frequency-notes
outputs.desc: How often and how substantially they give, measured the same way as the give side

process: For each relationship, list what they give you across the same categories. Use the give-inventory as a mirror, filling in the other direction for the same person so the two sides are directly comparable.

Pay special attention to the forms of value that are easy to take for granted: being reliably available, consistent emotional support, information and context you would not otherwise have, and access to their network.
Measure frequency and weight the same way you did for giving, so the comparison is fair. A friend who gives steady low-key support may out-give a contact who did one flashy favor.

Correct the opposite bias here. People who undercount their own giving often also undercount what they receive, and people who feel over-given-to often fail to see the quiet value flowing back to them.

steps.description: Assess the balance of each relationship by comparing the give and receive inventories, mapping the direction and degree of value flow, while accounting for the fact that healthy relationships balance over time rather than in every single exchange.

inputs.name: receive-inventory
inputs.desc: What each person gives you

inputs.name: receive-frequency-notes
inputs.desc: Frequency and weight of what they give

outputs.name: balance-ratios
outputs.desc: For each relationship, a rough reading of balance: roughly even, you give more, or they give more, and by how much

outputs.name: flow-direction-map
outputs.desc: The net direction of value flow across the mapped network, showing where you are a net giver and net receiver

process: For each relationship, compare the two inventories and read the balance qualitatively: roughly even, tilted toward you giving more, or tilted toward them giving more. Avoid false precision, a direction and a rough degree is enough.

Judge balance over time, not per exchange. Healthy relationships are not tit-for-tat, they even out across months and years. A relationship that looks lopsided this month may be balanced across the year, so take the longer view.
Account for different currencies. One person gives money and the other gives time, and that can be a fair trade. Imbalance is when the total value is lopsided, not when the currencies differ.

Map the net direction across the whole set. Seeing where you are a net giver and where a net receiver across the network reveals patterns a single relationship hides, like giving generously to people who cannot reciprocate while under-investing in peers who could.

steps.description: Classify the imbalanced relationships into where you over-give and where you under-give, and diagnose why, because the cause (generosity, people-pleasing, status-seeking, simple neglect) determines whether and how to rebalance.

inputs.name: balance-ratios
inputs.desc: Balance reading per relationship

inputs.name: flow-direction-map
inputs.desc: Net direction of value flow across the network

outputs.name: over-give-list
outputs.desc: Relationships where you give substantially more than you receive, with the likely cause

outputs.name: under-give-list
outputs.desc: Relationships where you receive substantially more than you give, with the likely cause

process: Pull the clearly imbalanced relationships into two lists. Leave the roughly-even ones alone, they are working. The energy goes to the lopsided ones.

For each over-give relationship, diagnose why you give more. Sometimes it is chosen generosity toward someone who genuinely cannot reciprocate (a mentee, a relative in need), which is healthy. Sometimes it is people-pleasing or buying approval, which is not. The distinction decides whether to act.

For each under-give relationship, diagnose why you receive more. Often it is simple neglect of someone generous, which is a quiet risk because under-given people eventually withdraw without announcing it. Sometimes you are early in a relationship where the balance has not formed yet.

Flag the dangerous cases: chronic over-giving that is draining you, and chronic under-receiving where a generous person is being taken for granted. These are the unstable relationships most likely to break if left alone.

steps.description: Build a rebalancing plan for the imbalanced relationships: give more where you have been coasting on others' generosity, and pull back or reset expectations where you have been over-giving, with care, since abruptly changing the terms of a relationship can itself cause harm.

inputs.name: over-give-list
inputs.desc: Relationships where you give more, with cause

inputs.name: under-give-list
inputs.desc: Relationships where you receive more, with cause

outputs.name: rebalance-actions
outputs.desc: Specific actions per relationship: concrete ways to give more to under-given people and to adjust over-giving

outputs.name: rebalance-cautions
outputs.desc: Where to move gently, since changing established terms can be read as withdrawal or rejection if done abruptly

process: For under-give relationships, plan specific ways to give back drawn from the value lens: make the introduction you have been meaning to make, offer the help they would value, reciprocate the support they have given. Vague intent to be better does not rebalance anything.

For unhealthy over-giving, plan to reduce gradually and redirect the freed energy. The goal is not to start keeping score with a friend, it is to stop over-investing where it drains you and reinvest where the balance is real.
Leave chosen generosity alone. Where you give more on purpose to someone who cannot reciprocate and you are glad to, that is not an imbalance to fix, and the plan should explicitly protect it.

Move gently where you are changing established terms. A person used to your over-giving may read a sudden pullback as rejection, so reset expectations slowly and, where appropriate, honestly, rather than withdrawing abruptly and leaving them confused.

description: Find the structural holes in your network using Burt's structural holes theory. Map your network into clusters, find where you have zero connections, and recognize that those gaps are opportunities and information you will never hear about because no one in your network is positioned to tell you. Then fill one gap at a time by joining the communities your existing network does not reach, rather than adding more contacts in the clusters where you are already saturated.

steps.description: Map your network into clusters by shared context (employer, industry, school, geography, community), because the structural view that reveals gaps requires seeing your network as a set of groups rather than a flat list of individuals.

inputs.name: contact-list
inputs.desc: Your contacts with enough metadata to group them: how you know them, their industry, role, and location

inputs.name: clustering-basis
inputs.desc: The dimensions to cluster on: shared employer, industry, profession, school, geography, social community

outputs.name: cluster-map
outputs.desc: Your network grouped into clusters, each a set of contacts who share a context and who mostly know each other

outputs.name: cluster-labels
outputs.desc: A label and rough size for each cluster, with a note on how connected its members are to each other

process: Group your contacts by shared context. Most people cluster naturally: current coworkers, former coworkers, an industry group, a school cohort, a geographic community, a hobby or social circle.
Label each cluster and estimate its size. The size matters because a very large cluster is where you are probably over-invested, and a thin cluster may be a bridge worth strengthening.

Note internal density, how much the members of a cluster know each other. A dense cluster (everyone knows everyone) gives you redundant information, because anything one member knows the others likely know too.
Identify which clusters you personally bridge, where you are the main link between two groups. Those bridges are a source of your value, and they are also fragile, which later steps address.

steps.description: Find the regions where you have zero connections: the industries, roles, communities, and worlds your network does not touch at all. These blind spots are invisible from inside your network precisely because no one in it can point them out to you.

inputs.name: cluster-map
inputs.desc: Your network grouped into clusters

inputs.name: cluster-labels
inputs.desc: Labels, sizes, and internal density of each cluster

outputs.name: zero-connection-regions
outputs.desc: The worlds you have no path into: industries, functions, seniority levels, geographies, or communities absent from your clusters

outputs.name: missing-cluster-list
outputs.desc: The specific clusters that should plausibly exist in your network given your goals but do not

process: Step back from the clusters you have and ask what is not there. List the industries, professional functions, seniority levels, geographies, and communities that are absent entirely from your map.

Reason from your goals to the clusters you would expect to need. If a goal depends on reaching a world (a new industry, a type of role, a funding source) and no cluster touches it, that is a structural gap, not a minor omission.

Accept that this step is inherently hard, because you are trying to see what you cannot see. Use external references (industry maps, org structures, who normally surrounds a goal like yours) to surface worlds you would not think of unprompted.

Distinguish gaps that matter from gaps that do not. You do not need to know everyone in every field. A missing cluster is only a real gap if it sits between you and something you want or need to hear about.

steps.description: Value each gap by what filling it would give you access to, and prioritize, since a network has more gaps than anyone can fill and the structural holes worth bridging are the ones connected to real opportunities or to resilience against a real risk.

inputs.name: zero-connection-regions
inputs.desc: The worlds your network does not touch

inputs.name: missing-cluster-list
inputs.desc: Clusters that should plausibly exist but do not

outputs.name: gap-value-scores
outputs.desc: Each gap scored by the value of what it would open up: information, opportunities, or resilience

outputs.name: prioritized-gaps
outputs.desc: The gaps ranked, so attention goes to the few highest-value holes rather than spreading thin

process: For each gap, name concretely what filling it would give you: information you currently cannot get, opportunities you cannot currently reach, or resilience against a risk your current clusters all share.

Apply Burt's core insight, that the value of a structural hole is the non-redundant information and opportunity on the other side. A gap into a world that thinks differently from all your clusters is worth more than one into a near-duplicate of what you have.

Weigh resilience, not just opportunity. If all your high-trust relationships sit in one industry or one employer, the gap into a different world is worth filling as insurance, because a single downturn could otherwise take out your whole network at once.
Rank the gaps and keep the priority list short. Filling one gap well, by genuinely entering a new community, takes months, so three prioritized gaps is plenty to work on at a time.

steps.description: For the prioritized gaps, identify the actual communities, venues, and groups where the people on the other side gather, turning an abstract gap into a concrete place you could show up, since you fill a gap by entering a community, not by collecting individual contacts.

inputs.name: gap-value-scores
inputs.desc: Each gap scored by the value it would open up

inputs.name: prioritized-gaps
inputs.desc: The gaps ranked by priority

outputs.name: candidate-communities
outputs.desc: For each prioritized gap, the specific communities, events, groups, or venues where those people actually gather

outputs.name: community-access-notes
outputs.desc: How open each community is to newcomers and what it takes to enter credibly

process: For each prioritized gap, find where those people actually congregate: professional associations, conferences, online communities, local meetups, alumni groups, or recurring events specific to that world.

Rank candidate communities by the ratio of target people present to the effort of entering. A focused community full of the people you want to reach beats a large general venue where they are a small fraction.

Note each community's openness. Some welcome newcomers immediately, some require a credential or an invitation, some expect you to contribute before you belong. The access path shapes the entry strategy.

Prefer communities where you can genuinely contribute, not just extract. You enter a community credibly by being useful in it, and a community you join only to mine for contacts will sense it and keep you at the edge.

steps.description: Select one gap to work on first, against the discipline of filling gaps one at a time, because genuine entry into a new community demands sustained presence and spreading yourself across several at once produces shallow presence in all of them and real entry into none.

inputs.name: candidate-communities
inputs.desc: Communities where the target people gather, per gap

inputs.name: community-access-notes
inputs.desc: How open each community is and what entry takes

outputs.name: selected-gap
outputs.desc: The single gap to fill first, with its chosen target community

outputs.name: selection-rationale
outputs.desc: Why this gap and community first: value, accessibility, and fit with your current capacity

process: Choose one gap. The temptation is to start on several at once, but entering a community well takes repeated presence over months, and parallel attempts dilute into shallow dabbling that reaches no community.

Balance value against accessibility and your current capacity. The highest-value gap is not always the right first move if its community is hard to enter and you have little time. An accessible medium-value gap can be the better starting point to build momentum.
Pick the specific community within the gap, not just the gap. The target is show up at this group, not break into this industry. Concreteness is what makes the next step actionable.
Write down why this one first. When the entry gets slow, as it will, the rationale reminds you why you chose it and keeps you from abandoning it to chase a shinier gap before this one has paid off.

steps.description: Design the entry strategy for the selected community: how you will show up, contribute, and build initial relationships so you enter as a genuine participant rather than an outsider collecting contacts, because the quality of entry determines whether the gap actually closes.

inputs.name: selected-gap
inputs.desc: The single gap and its target community

inputs.name: selection-rationale
inputs.desc: Why this gap and community were chosen first

outputs.name: entry-plan
outputs.desc: The concrete plan to enter the community: how to show up, how to contribute, and the cadence of presence

outputs.name: first-contact-targets
outputs.desc: The first few people to build real relationships with inside the community, chosen as footholds rather than trophies

process: Plan how you will show up and keep showing up. One appearance at an event does not enter a community. Decide the cadence (attend the monthly meetup, post regularly in the forum, volunteer for the association) that builds familiarity over time.

Lead with contribution. Decide what you can offer this community that is genuinely useful (knowledge, help, effort, a connection from your other clusters). Contribution is what converts you from visitor to member.

Choose a few first-contact targets as footholds, not trophies. The welcoming regular, the organizer, the fellow newcomer are better early relationships than the most senior person, because they integrate you into the community rather than giving you one isolated contact.

Set a realistic time horizon. Genuine entry typically takes months of repeated presence, so plan for that rather than expecting a few weeks to close a structural hole, and judge progress by relationships formed, not events attended.

steps.description: Track progress on closing the selected gap and decide when it is filled enough to move to the next one, so gap-filling becomes an ongoing practice that keeps your network structurally healthy rather than a one-time project that quietly lapses.

inputs.name: entry-plan
inputs.desc: The plan to enter and contribute to the community

inputs.name: first-contact-targets
inputs.desc: The first foothold relationships inside the community

outputs.name: gap-fill-tracker
outputs.desc: A simple tracker of entry progress: presence maintained, relationships formed, and whether the gap is beginning to deliver its value

outputs.name: progress-review-cadence
outputs.desc: When to review progress, when to judge the gap filled enough, and when to begin the next gap

process: Track the inputs you control: whether you are maintaining the planned presence and contribution. Showing up as planned is the leading indicator, because relationships and value follow from consistent presence, not from intention.

Track the outputs that signal the gap is closing: real relationships forming (people who now recognize and respond to you), and the first non-redundant information or opportunity reaching you through the new community.

Define filled enough rather than finished. A gap is filled when you have a few genuine relationships in the community and value has started to flow, at which point the community largely sustains itself with lighter upkeep.

Set a review cadence to decide when to start the next prioritized gap, and fold the filled gap into ordinary relationship maintenance so it does not decay back into a hole while your attention moves on.

description: After a life change (a move, a job change, a breakup, a loss, becoming a parent, a health event) triage your relationships with three questions: does this person give or drain energy, is there mutual investment, and does this relationship align with who you are becoming. Sort each relationship into keep, maintain with boundaries, or let go gracefully. A life change is the natural moment to do this consciously instead of letting relationships drift by default.

steps.description: Inventory the relationships to triage and capture how the life change has already shifted each one, because a major change tends to rearrange relationships on its own (some deepen, some strain, some lose their shared basis) and the triage works with that movement rather than against it.

inputs.name: life-change-context
inputs.desc: The life change prompting the triage and how it has altered your circumstances, priorities, and available time

inputs.name: relationship-pool
inputs.desc: The relationships currently in your life, across personal, family, social, and professional spheres

outputs.name: triage-inventory
outputs.desc: The relationships to triage, with the ones most affected by the change noted

outputs.name: change-impact-notes
outputs.desc: How the life change has already shifted each relationship: strengthened, strained, or lost its shared basis

process: List the relationships that are active or lingering in your life right now across every sphere, including the ones that feel obligatory and the ones running purely on momentum.

Note how the change has affected each. A move strains proximity-based friendships, a job change dissolves relationships built only on shared work, a loss or a health event reveals who shows up. The change has already begun sorting them.
Mark the relationships most disrupted by the change, because those are where conscious triage matters most. Relationships untouched by the change can mostly continue as they are.

Approach the inventory without guilt. A life change legitimately reshapes a social world, and some relationships ending is natural rather than a failure. The triage names that honestly instead of letting it happen by neglect.

steps.description: Ask the first triage question of each relationship: on balance, does this person give energy or drain it? This is the most immediate signal and the easiest to read honestly after a life change, when your energy is often limited and you can feel clearly which interactions restore you and which deplete you.

inputs.name: triage-inventory
inputs.desc: The relationships to triage

inputs.name: change-impact-notes
inputs.desc: How the change has shifted each relationship

outputs.name: energy-assessments
outputs.desc: Each relationship marked as net energy-giving, neutral, or net energy-draining, over a fair sample of interactions

outputs.name: energy-flagged-relationships
outputs.desc: The clearly draining relationships flagged for closer examination in the later questions

process: For each relationship, recall how you feel after your typical interactions, not your best or worst single memory. Energized and lighter, neutral, or depleted and heavier is the reading you want.
Judge over a fair sample. Everyone has an off day, and a good relationship going through a hard stretch is not a draining one. Look at the pattern across many interactions, not a recent rough patch.

Separate draining from demanding. A relationship that asks a lot but that you choose to pour into (a child, a friend in crisis) can be demanding without being draining, because the giving is meaningful. Draining is when you leave consistently depleted with nothing gained.

Flag the consistently draining relationships. A drain is not an automatic cut, since the later questions may reveal real mutual investment or alignment, but it is the signal that this relationship needs a conscious decision rather than default continuation.

steps.description: Ask the second triage question: is the investment mutual, or are you the only one maintaining the relationship? Mutual investment is what distinguishes a relationship worth sustaining through a hard stretch from one that only exists because you keep it alive single-handedly.

inputs.name: energy-assessments
inputs.desc: Energy reading per relationship

inputs.name: energy-flagged-relationships
inputs.desc: The clearly draining relationships flagged

outputs.name: investment-assessments
outputs.desc: Each relationship marked by whether investment is mutual, mostly one-way toward you, or mostly one-way from you

outputs.name: one-sided-flags
outputs.desc: Relationships you maintain entirely alone, where the other person never initiates or reciprocates

process: For each relationship, ask who initiates and who reciprocates. Do they reach out, remember what matters to you, and show up, or does the relationship only happen when you drive it?

Be fair about circumstance. Someone going through their own hard period may invest less temporarily while still being genuinely invested. One-sidedness is a concern when it is the enduring pattern, not a season.

Distinguish the two directions of one-sidedness. A relationship where you give far more than you get is a different problem from one where someone depends heavily on you, and both differ from mutual investment.

Flag the relationships you maintain entirely alone. A relationship that would simply end the moment you stopped initiating is telling you something, and the life change is the moment to decide whether to keep carrying it or let it rest.

steps.description: Ask the third triage question: does this relationship align with who you are becoming? A life change often shifts your direction, and some relationships fit the person you were while others fit the person you are growing into. Alignment is the hardest question because a relationship can be energy-giving and mutual yet still belong to a chapter that is closing.

inputs.name: investment-assessments
inputs.desc: Mutual-investment reading per relationship

inputs.name: one-sided-flags
inputs.desc: Relationships you maintain entirely alone

outputs.name: alignment-assessments
outputs.desc: Each relationship marked by how well it fits the direction you are growing toward after the change

outputs.name: alignment-conflicts
outputs.desc: Relationships that are positive on energy and investment but pull against who you are becoming

process: For each relationship, ask whether it supports the direction you are heading or holds you in a version of yourself you are leaving behind. Some relationships are anchored to habits, places, or identities that the change is moving you past.

Be honest about relationships that keep you in old patterns. A relationship can be comfortable and even positive and still quietly anchor you to a self you are trying to grow out of, which is the subtlest finding in the triage.

Do not confuse alignment with usefulness. This is about whether the relationship fits your life and values going forward, not whether the person is advantageous. A deep friendship that spans many chapters aligns even if it serves no purpose.

Flag the alignment conflicts: relationships that score well on energy and mutual investment yet pull against your direction. These are the genuinely hard calls, and the disposition step addresses them with options beyond a simple keep or cut.

steps.description: Combine the three answers into a disposition for each relationship: keep (invest fully), maintain with boundaries (continue in a limited, defined way), or let go gracefully. The middle option matters most, since most relationships are not clean keeps or clean cuts and deserve a defined, limited place rather than an all-or-nothing verdict.

inputs.name: alignment-assessments
inputs.desc: Alignment reading per relationship

inputs.name: alignment-conflicts
inputs.desc: Positive relationships that conflict with your direction

outputs.name: disposition-assignments
outputs.desc: Each relationship assigned keep, maintain with boundaries, or let go gracefully, based on the three questions together

outputs.name: boundary-notes
outputs.desc: For the maintain-with-boundaries group, the specific limits that let the relationship continue without the cost that triggered the flag

process: Combine the three readings. A relationship that gives energy, is mutual, and aligns is a clear keep. One that drains, is one-sided, and misaligns is a clear let-go. Most relationships land somewhere between, which is where the middle option does its work.

Assign maintain-with-boundaries to the mixed cases: the family member you will not cut but whose draining patterns you will limit, the old friend you will see occasionally but no longer center, the alignment conflict you keep in a smaller role.

For each maintain-with-boundaries relationship, define the actual boundary: how often, in what contexts, with what topics off limits, with what level of investment. A boundary that is only a vague intention does not hold.

Resist resolving every hard case as a cut. Letting go is right for some, but the maintain-with-boundaries option preserves relationships that are worth a limited place, which an all-or-nothing triage would wrongly destroy.

steps.description: For the let-go group, plan a graceful exit, because how a relationship ends matters and most relationships deserve a gentle fade or an honest close rather than a cruel cutoff or a cowardly ghosting. The aim is to release the relationship without inflicting unnecessary harm on the other person or on your own peace.

inputs.name: disposition-assignments
inputs.desc: The keep, maintain, and let-go assignments

inputs.name: boundary-notes
inputs.desc: The boundaries defined for the maintain-with-boundaries group

outputs.name: exit-plans
outputs.desc: For each let-go relationship, how it will end: a natural fade, an honest conversation, or a clear boundary, matched to the relationship

outputs.name: closure-scripts
outputs.desc: What to say where an explicit close is warranted, said with honesty and without blame

process: Match the exit to the relationship. A casual relationship can simply fade as you stop initiating, and forcing a dramatic conversation on it would be odd. A close or formal relationship warrants an honest ending rather than a silent fade.

Choose honesty over ghosting for relationships that mattered. Disappearing on someone who was genuinely part of your life leaves them with an open loop and leaves you with guilt. A brief honest close serves both of you better.

Where an explicit close is warranted, prepare what to say so it lands with care: honest about the relationship changing, free of blame, and without relitigating old grievances. The goal is release, not a verdict on who was wrong.

Protect your own peace in the plan. Some relationships cannot be ended cleanly because the other person will not allow it, and in those cases a firm boundary (or, in genuinely harmful cases, a clean break) is the graceful option available to you.

description: Map the people who affect a decision or project. For each: their position (supportive, neutral, or opposed), what they actually care about, what would move them, and who influences them. Then sequence your effort: convert the neutrals first (they are cheapest to move and shift the center of gravity), and only then address the opposed. Most people either ignore stakeholder dynamics entirely or spend all their energy arguing with the most vocal opponent, which is usually the worst allocation of effort.

steps.description: Identify everyone who affects or is affected by the decision or project, including the quiet influencers who hold no formal role but shape the outcome, because the stakeholder who sinks a project is often the one nobody put on the list.

inputs.name: decision-or-project
inputs.desc: The decision or project whose stakeholders you are mapping, and the outcome you want

inputs.name: scope-notes
inputs.desc: The boundaries of the effort: what it touches, whose work or interests it changes, and who holds approval or veto

outputs.name: stakeholder-list
outputs.desc: Everyone who affects or is affected by the outcome, formal and informal

outputs.name: stakeholder-roles
outputs.desc: Each stakeholder's relationship to the decision: decision-maker, approver, influencer, implementer, or affected party
