process: List the obvious stakeholders first: the formal decision-makers, approvers, and the people whose work the outcome directly changes.

Then hunt for the non-obvious ones: the trusted adviser a decision-maker always consults, the veteran whose opinion carries weight informally, the team that will have to live with the result and can quietly undermine it.

Classify each by their relationship to the decision: who decides, who must approve, who influences the deciders, who implements, and who is simply affected. The role determines how much their position matters.

Check for the invisible veto. Many efforts fail because of a stakeholder with no formal authority but real informal power to block, so deliberately ask who could kill this quietly and make sure they are on the list.

steps.description: Classify each stakeholder's current position toward the outcome as supportive, neutral, or opposed, and rate your confidence, because position is often misread (public agreement can mask private opposition) and acting on a wrong read wastes effort or triggers an ambush.

inputs.name: stakeholder-list
inputs.desc: Everyone who affects or is affected by the outcome

inputs.name: stakeholder-roles
inputs.desc: Each stakeholder's role relative to the decision

outputs.name: position-map
outputs.desc: Each stakeholder marked supportive, neutral, or opposed toward the outcome you want

outputs.name: position-confidence
outputs.desc: How confident you are in each read, flagging the ones based on assumption rather than evidence

process: Mark each stakeholder supportive, neutral, or opposed based on what you actually know, not on what their role suggests they should think. People surprise you in both directions.

Rate your confidence in each read. A position you have heard them state is high confidence, a position you are inferring from their incentives is a guess, and guesses need verification before you build a plan on them.

Watch for the gap between public and private positions. Someone agreeable in meetings may be privately opposed and working against the effort quietly, which is far more dangerous than open opposition.

Flag the low-confidence reads for direct checking. Where a stakeholder is important and your read is a guess, finding out their real position (through conversation or a trusted intermediary) is worth doing before you plan around an assumption.

steps.description: Map what each stakeholder actually cares about, separating their stated position from the underlying interest driving it, because people take positions for reasons, and you move a position only by addressing the interest beneath it, not by arguing against the position itself.

inputs.name: position-map
inputs.desc: Each stakeholder's position toward the outcome

inputs.name: position-confidence
inputs.desc: Confidence in each position read

outputs.name: interest-map
outputs.desc: For each stakeholder, the underlying interests driving their position: what they protect, want, fear, or are measured on

outputs.name: stated-vs-real-interests
outputs.desc: Where a stakeholder's stated reason differs from the real interest, so you address the right thing

process: For each stakeholder, dig past the position to the interest. Someone opposing a change may really be protecting their team's workload, their status, a metric they are judged on, or simply their sense of control. The position is the symptom.

Distinguish stated reasons from real interests. The stated objection (this is technically risky) often masks the real one (this threatens my role). Addressing the stated reason while missing the real one changes nothing.

Identify what each stakeholder is measured and rewarded on, because self-interest around incentives drives more positions than people admit. A stakeholder whose bonus depends on a metric your project threatens will oppose it regardless of its merits.

Note the interests you can genuinely serve versus those you cannot. Some opposition rests on interests you can accommodate, and some on interests fundamentally at odds with the outcome, and knowing which is which shapes whether to convert or to route around them.

steps.description: For each stakeholder, identify the lever that would actually move their position: the evidence, assurance, accommodation, or trade that addresses their real interest. A lever is specific and grounded in their interest, not a generic case for why the outcome is good.

inputs.name: interest-map
inputs.desc: The underlying interests driving each position

inputs.name: stated-vs-real-interests
inputs.desc: Where stated reasons differ from real interests

outputs.name: movement-levers
outputs.desc: For each stakeholder, the specific thing that would move them toward support: evidence, an assurance, an accommodation, a trade, or a trusted endorsement

outputs.name: lever-evidence
outputs.desc: What you would need to supply or demonstrate for each lever to work

process: For each stakeholder, design the lever from their interest. If the interest is a protected workload, the lever is a credible assurance or a resource that protects it. If it is a metric, the lever is evidence the outcome improves or does not harm that metric.

Make levers specific to the person, not generic. The same project moves different stakeholders through different levers, and a one-size pitch persuades no one because it addresses no one's actual interest.

Prefer levers you can actually deliver. A lever that requires promising something you cannot guarantee buys short-term agreement and long-term distrust, so ground each lever in what you can genuinely provide.

Identify what each lever requires you to supply: the data to gather, the assurance to secure, the accommodation to arrange, or the trusted person whose endorsement would carry weight. The lever is only useful once you can actually pull it.

steps.description: Map who influences whom among the stakeholders, because positions are not held in isolation: many stakeholders take their cue from someone they trust, and moving that trusted influencer can shift several positions at once far more efficiently than persuading each person directly.

inputs.name: movement-levers
inputs.desc: The lever that would move each stakeholder

inputs.name: lever-evidence
inputs.desc: What each lever requires you to supply

outputs.name: influence-network
outputs.desc: The map of who influences whom among the stakeholders, showing whose opinion others follow

outputs.name: influencer-ranking
outputs.desc: The stakeholders whose position shifts the most other positions, ranked by reach

process: Map the influence ties: for each stakeholder, note whose lead they follow, whose opinion they check, and who they defer to. Influence often runs along lines of trust and expertise, not the org chart.

Find the high-leverage influencers, the stakeholders whose shift would cascade. A respected skeptic who comes around can bring several fence-sitters with them, which is far cheaper than converting each one directly.
Account for the influence the opposed hold. An opponent who influences several neutrals is more dangerous than an isolated one, because they are not just one position against you, they anchor others.
Rank stakeholders by influence reach, not just by their own position. This ranking reorders your effort: a neutral with wide influence may deserve more attention than a supporter with none.

steps.description: Build the plan to convert the neutrals first, because neutrals are the cheapest to move (they are not invested in opposing you), converting them builds visible momentum, and shifting the center of gravity toward support often makes the opposed far easier to handle afterward.

inputs.name: influence-network
inputs.desc: Who influences whom among stakeholders

inputs.name: influencer-ranking
inputs.desc: Stakeholders ranked by influence reach

outputs.name: neutral-conversion-plan
outputs.desc: The plan to move the neutrals to support, prioritizing high-influence neutrals and using each one's specific lever

outputs.name: conversion-sequence
outputs.desc: The order of approach, sequenced so early conversions build momentum and influence toward the harder ones

process: Start with the neutrals, not the loudest opponent. Neutrals are cheaper to move because they hold no stake in opposing you, and a visible run of neutrals turning supportive shifts the perceived consensus.

Prioritize high-influence neutrals using the influence map, because converting one neutral who sways three others is worth more than converting three isolated ones. Apply each neutral's specific lever from the lever step.

Sequence the approach so momentum compounds. Convert the accessible, high-influence neutrals first, let their visible support make the next ones easier, and build toward a tipping point where support looks like the default position.

Track the shifting center of gravity. As neutrals convert, the opposed increasingly find themselves isolated rather than leading a faction, which is exactly the condition under which the opposition-handling step becomes manageable.

steps.description: Build the plan to address the opposed, now that the neutrals have shifted the balance, choosing deliberately for each opponent among genuine conversion, negotiated accommodation, containment, or routing around them, since not every opponent can or needs to be won over.

inputs.name: neutral-conversion-plan
inputs.desc: The plan and sequence for converting neutrals

inputs.name: conversion-sequence
inputs.desc: The order of approach that builds momentum

outputs.name: opposition-handling-plan
outputs.desc: For each opponent, the chosen approach: convert via their lever, negotiate an accommodation, contain their influence, or route around them

outputs.name: escalation-guardrails
outputs.desc: The limits on how far to push, so handling opposition does not create lasting enemies or a damaging fight

process: Address the opposed only after the neutrals have moved, because an opponent isolated from the fence-sitters they used to anchor is far more tractable than one leading a faction.

Choose an approach per opponent rather than defaulting to persuasion. Convert the ones whose interest you can genuinely serve, negotiate an accommodation with those who need something specific, contain the influence of those you cannot move, and simply route around the ones whose opposition does not actually block the outcome.
Know when not to fight. Energy spent arguing with an implacable low-influence opponent is energy wasted, and some opposition is best left alone once it can no longer sway the decision.

Set guardrails on escalation. Winning the decision while making a lasting enemy of someone you will work with again is often a net loss, so decide in advance how hard to push and preserve the relationship where you can, because today's opponent is tomorrow's stakeholder on another project.

description: Build a follow-up system on one principle: after every meaningful interaction, capture one concrete action within 24 hours, schedule it with a specific date, and track it to completion. Consistent follow-up is the highest-return relationship behavior there is, because it is rare, it signals reliability, and it compounds. The system makes follow-up automatic rather than dependent on memory and good intentions.

steps.description: Design the capture protocol that gets a follow-up out of your head and into the system within 24 hours of an interaction, because the window in which you remember what was said and what you intended to do closes fast, and a follow-up not captured in that window is usually lost.

inputs.name: interaction-types
inputs.desc: The kinds of interactions that generate follow-ups: meetings, calls, chance conversations, messages, events

inputs.name: capture-tools
inputs.desc: The tools available to capture into: a task app, a notes app, voice memo, a CRM, a notebook

outputs.name: capture-protocol
outputs.desc: The protocol for capturing a follow-up right after an interaction, tuned to each interaction type

outputs.name: capture-window-rules
outputs.desc: The rule that follow-ups are captured within 24 hours, with the practical trigger that enforces it

process: Set the core rule: capture within 24 hours, ideally within minutes. The memory of what mattered and what you meant to do decays quickly, and a vague recollection a week later is not enough to act on.

Design capture per interaction type. A scheduled meeting can end with two minutes of capture built in, a chance conversation needs an immediate voice memo or note before the next thing crowds it out, a message thread can be captured as you close it.

Choose the lowest-friction tool you will actually use in the moment. The best capture tool is the one already in your hand, so a quick note or voice memo beats a polished system you have to sit down to open.

Attach capture to an existing trigger so it does not depend on remembering to remember: the act of leaving a meeting, hanging up a call, or closing a conversation becomes the cue to capture before moving on.

steps.description: Define how to extract the one concrete action from an interaction, because most interactions generate a vague sense of I should follow up rather than a specific doable task, and a follow-up that is not a concrete action never gets done.

inputs.name: capture-protocol
inputs.desc: The protocol for capturing follow-ups after interactions

inputs.name: capture-window-rules
inputs.desc: The 24 hour capture window and its trigger

outputs.name: action-extraction-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for turning what happened in an interaction into one specific, doable follow-up action

outputs.name: action-quality-criteria
outputs.desc: The test for whether a captured follow-up is concrete enough to act on without further thinking

process: Extract one action, not a list. A single clear follow-up that actually happens beats five good intentions that do not. If an interaction genuinely generated several, pick the one that matters most and let the rest go.
Make the action concrete and self-contained. Not follow up with Sarah but send Sarah the article on route planning we discussed. The captured task should require no further thinking to execute.
Capture the context the action needs alongside it: what was discussed, what you promised, and any detail you will need, so that future-you can act without reconstructing the conversation.

Apply a quality test to each captured action: could you do this right now from the capture alone, without remembering anything extra? If not, it is too vague, and you sharpen it while the interaction is still fresh.

steps.description: Define how every follow-up gets a specific date rather than living on an undated someday list, because an undated follow-up is not scheduled, it is merely hoped for, and the specific date is what moves it from intention to commitment.

inputs.name: action-extraction-rules
inputs.desc: Rules for extracting one concrete follow-up action

inputs.name: action-quality-criteria
inputs.desc: The test for whether an action is concrete enough

outputs.name: scheduling-rules
outputs.desc: Rules for assigning every follow-up a specific do-date, including how to time follow-ups appropriately

outputs.name: due-date-logic
outputs.desc: How to set the date based on urgency, the promise made, and the natural rhythm of the relationship

process: Require a specific date on every follow-up. Someday is not a date, and a task without a date drifts indefinitely. Even a rough but specific date (next Tuesday) is a commitment where someday is not.

Time the follow-up appropriately rather than always immediately. Some follow-ups are urgent (a promise to send something today), some are better paced (a check-in that would feel pushy the next day but natural in two weeks). The date reflects the right timing, not just the soonest.

Honor any timing you committed to. If you told someone you would follow up after their launch, the date is after their launch, not whenever you remember. The specific date is how you keep the implicit promise.
Put the dated follow-up where it will surface on its day: a task manager with due dates, a calendar, or a tickler system. A date that does not resurface the task when it comes due is just a note.

steps.description: Build the tracking that ensures scheduled follow-ups actually get completed and that overdue ones get caught rather than silently abandoned, because a follow-up system that captures and schedules but does not enforce completion just produces a well-organized list of broken intentions.

inputs.name: scheduling-rules
inputs.desc: Rules for assigning follow-ups specific dates

inputs.name: due-date-logic
inputs.desc: How dates are set based on urgency and relationship rhythm

outputs.name: completion-tracker
outputs.desc: The mechanism for seeing follow-ups due today, marking them done, and spotting what slipped

outputs.name: overdue-escalation-rules
outputs.desc: What happens to an overdue follow-up: reschedule with intent, do it now, or consciously drop it

process: Build a daily view of follow-ups due today, so working the system is a short routine (see what is due, do it or reschedule it) rather than an open-ended search through a backlog.
Mark completion explicitly. The act of marking a follow-up done both clears it and gives you a visible record of reliability, which is the evidence the review step uses later.
Catch the overdue rather than letting them vanish. An overdue follow-up should resurface, not disappear, because the whole value of the system is that nothing meant to happen quietly fails to.

Set an honest rule for overdue items: either reschedule with a real new date and intent, do it now, or consciously drop it and let the person go. An item rescheduled five times is one you have decided not to do, and naming that is better than carrying it as permanent guilt.

steps.description: Review the return the follow-up system is producing, because seeing that consistent follow-up actually strengthens relationships and opens opportunities is what sustains the habit, and the review also reveals where follow-up is being spent on low-value interactions and where it is missing high-value ones.

inputs.name: completion-tracker
inputs.desc: The record of follow-ups due, done, and slipped

inputs.name: overdue-escalation-rules
inputs.desc: How overdue follow-ups are handled

outputs.name: roi-review-method
outputs.desc: A periodic review of what the follow-up system is producing: relationships strengthened, opportunities opened, reliability demonstrated

outputs.name: follow-through-metrics
outputs.desc: The few numbers worth watching: follow-up completion rate, average time from capture to completion, and share of meaningful interactions that generated a follow-up

process: Review periodically what the follow-ups produced. Note the relationships that deepened, the opportunities that came from a reliable follow-up, and the trust built by consistently doing what you said you would. Seeing the return sustains the habit.
Track completion rate as the core health metric. A high rate means the system is real, a falling rate means capture or scheduling is breaking down and the habit is slipping.
Watch the time from capture to completion. Follow-ups that routinely complete long after their date point to dates set unrealistically or a tracker that is not surfacing them, both fixable.

Check where follow-up is being allocated. If you are diligently following up on low-value interactions while high-value ones generate no follow-up, the fix is in what you choose to capture, not in working the system harder.

steps.description: Install follow-up as a durable habit by reducing friction at every step and anchoring the behavior to existing routines, because the system only delivers its compounding return if it runs automatically, and a follow-up practice that depends on willpower eventually lapses.

inputs.name: roi-review-method
inputs.desc: The method for reviewing what follow-up produces

inputs.name: follow-through-metrics
inputs.desc: The numbers that indicate follow-up health

outputs.name: habit-install-plan
outputs.desc: A plan to make follow-up automatic: triggers, routines, and an initial period of deliberate practice

outputs.name: friction-reduction-steps
outputs.desc: Specific changes that lower the effort of capturing, scheduling, and completing follow-ups

process: Anchor each part of the system to an existing routine. Capture anchors to ending an interaction, scheduling anchors to capture, and working the due list anchors to a fixed daily moment (such as the start of the workday) so none of it depends on remembering to begin.

Reduce friction everywhere. Pre-set templates for common follow-ups, a capture tool already open, a one-tap way to mark done. Every bit of friction is a point where the habit can break, so removing friction is how the habit survives.

Run a deliberate practice period of a few weeks where you consciously enforce the loop, because a habit needs repetition to become automatic, and the early period is where it is most fragile and most worth protecting.

Use the metrics from the review as the feedback that keeps the habit honest. A completion rate you check regularly is a gentle accountability that catches the slip before the practice quietly dies, and once the return is visible the habit largely sustains itself.

description: Repair a damaged relationship through a disciplined sequence: diagnose the damage from both perspectives, own your part without equivocation, ask what repair looks like to the other person rather than assuming, propose concrete behavioral changes, follow through visibly over time, and accept that some damage is permanent. The sequence matters because repair attempts usually fail at a predictable point: people apologize for their version of events, propose their idea of repair, and expect trust to return immediately, none of which works.

steps.description: Diagnose the damage honestly from your own perspective first: what happened, what you did, and what the real harm was, because a repair built on a vague or self-serving account of the damage will address the wrong thing, and you cannot own a part you have not clearly named.

inputs.name: relationship-background
inputs.desc: The history and nature of the relationship and why it matters enough to repair

inputs.name: incident-summary
inputs.desc: What happened, as best you can reconstruct it, including the events that led to the damage

outputs.name: self-perspective-diagnosis
outputs.desc: Your honest account of what happened and what the real damage to the relationship was

outputs.name: self-contribution-notes
outputs.desc: The specific things you did or failed to do that contributed, named plainly without justification

process: Reconstruct what happened as factually as you can, separating the events from your interpretation of them. The goal is an account you could state plainly, not a case for your own defense.

Name the real damage, which is usually about trust, respect, or safety rather than the surface incident. The argument was about a missed deadline, but the damage was the other person learning they could not rely on you.

List your specific contributions plainly: the things you did, the things you failed to do, the patterns you brought. Write them without the word but, because every justification you attach here is one you will leak later and undermine the repair.

Resist the pull to make yourself the misunderstood party. A diagnosis that conveniently concludes you were mostly right is not a diagnosis, it is a defense, and it guarantees the repair will fail at the ownership step.

steps.description: Diagnose the damage from the other person's perspective, genuinely reconstructing how the events looked and felt to them, because repair that addresses only your version of what happened misses the harm they actually experienced, and the gap between the two perspectives is usually where the repair lives.

inputs.name: self-perspective-diagnosis
inputs.desc: Your honest account of what happened and the damage

inputs.name: self-contribution-notes
inputs.desc: Your specific contributions to the damage

outputs.name: other-perspective-diagnosis
outputs.desc: A genuine reconstruction of how the events looked and felt from the other person's side

outputs.name: perspective-gap-map
outputs.desc: Where your account and their likely account diverge, which is where the real repair work sits

process: Reconstruct the events as they likely experienced them, not as you need them to have experienced them. Ask what they saw, what they felt, and what they concluded about you, drawing on what you know of them.

Take their harm seriously even where you think it is disproportionate. Whether their reaction seems fair is beside the point for repair, the point is that the harm is real to them and the relationship will not recover until it is addressed.

Map the gap between the two perspectives. Often each person is reacting to something the other does not even see, and naming that gap (you were hurt by X, which I did not realize mattered) is frequently the heart of the repair.

Where you genuinely cannot reconstruct their view, note it as something to learn rather than guess. The next step asks them directly, and an honest I am not sure how this looked to you beats a confident wrong assumption.

steps.description: Compose and deliver an ownership statement that takes responsibility for your part without equivocation, because the equivocating apology (I am sorry if you were hurt, I am sorry but you also) is the single most common point where repair attempts fail, since it signals you are still defending rather than owning.

inputs.name: other-perspective-diagnosis
inputs.desc: How the events looked and felt from their side

inputs.name: perspective-gap-map
inputs.desc: Where your account and theirs diverge

outputs.name: ownership-statement
outputs.desc: A clear statement taking responsibility for your specific part, naming the harm, without excuse or counter-accusation

outputs.name: non-equivocation-check
outputs.desc: The check that the statement contains no hidden defense: no if, no but, no shifting blame, no demand for immediate forgiveness

process: Build the statement from your contribution notes and their perspective: name specifically what you did, acknowledge the harm it caused them in their terms, and express genuine regret for it.

Strip out every equivocation. I am sorry if you felt that way is not ownership, it is a suggestion they overreacted. I am sorry but you also is a counter-attack wearing an apology. Cut the if, the but, and the and-you-too entirely.

Own only your part, and own it fully rather than partially. You are not responsible for their contribution and should not claim it, but the part that is yours gets owned without hedging, because partial ownership reads as negotiation.

Make no demand for forgiveness or immediate repair in return. The ownership stands on its own, and attaching so now we are good to it converts the apology into a transaction and tells them you want the discomfort over more than you want to repair the harm.

steps.description: Ask the other person what repair would actually look like to them, rather than assuming, because people need different things to rebuild (some need acknowledgment, some need changed behavior, some need time, some need a specific amends) and imposing your idea of repair often misses what they actually require.

inputs.name: ownership-statement
inputs.desc: The delivered statement of responsibility

inputs.name: non-equivocation-check
inputs.desc: The confirmation the statement held no hidden defense

outputs.name: repair-definition-questions
outputs.desc: The questions that invite the other person to define what rebuilding trust would require from you

outputs.name: listening-protocol
outputs.desc: How to receive their answer: without defending, bargaining, or correcting, even when it is hard to hear

process: Ask directly and openly what rebuilding would require. Questions like what would help, what do you need from me, and what would it take to trust me again hand them the definition of repair instead of you assuming it.

Be ready for a range of answers. Some people need only to feel heard, some need a concrete change, some need an amends, some need time and space, and some are not ready to answer yet. Each is legitimate and tells you what the repair actually is.

Set the listening protocol before you ask, because their answer may be hard to hear. The discipline is to receive it without defending, correcting their account, or negotiating the terms down. You asked, so you listen.
Accept that they may not know yet, or may need the question to sit. Pushing for an immediate answer serves your urgency, not their repair, so leave room for the question to be answered over time.

steps.description: Propose concrete behavioral changes that address what they said they need, because trust is rebuilt through changed behavior over time, not through words, and a vague promise to do better gives them nothing to observe, while a specific change gives them something they can actually watch for.

inputs.name: repair-definition-questions
inputs.desc: What the other person said repair would require

inputs.name: listening-protocol
inputs.desc: How their answer was received

outputs.name: behavioral-change-proposals
outputs.desc: Specific, observable changes in your behavior that address what they identified as needed

outputs.name: change-commitments
outputs.desc: The changes stated as commitments you can be held to, with enough specificity that they will be able to tell whether you kept them

process: Translate what they need into specific behaviors. Not I will be more reliable but I will confirm commitments in writing and tell you immediately if something is at risk. A change they can observe is worth more than a virtue they have to take on faith.

Propose changes that genuinely address their stated need, not changes that are easy for you but miss the point. If they needed to feel consulted, the change is about how you include them, not an unrelated gesture.

Commit only to changes you will actually sustain, because a repair promise you break confirms their worst conclusion and does more damage than the original injury. Under-promise and hold it rather than over-promise and fail.

State the commitments specifically enough to be checkable, so both of you know what keeping them looks like. Vague commitments cannot be observed, which means they cannot rebuild trust, because trust rebuilds precisely by them watching you keep a specific word.

steps.description: Follow through on the committed changes visibly and consistently over time, because trust is restored only by a pattern of kept commitments that the other person can see, and the repair is not the apology or the promise but the weeks and months of behavior that prove the promise was real.

inputs.name: behavioral-change-proposals
inputs.desc: The specific changes proposed

inputs.name: change-commitments
inputs.desc: The changes stated as checkable commitments

outputs.name: followthrough-plan
outputs.desc: The plan to sustain the committed changes over the time it takes for trust to rebuild, not just in the first days

outputs.name: visibility-markers
outputs.desc: How the kept commitments become observable to the other person without you demanding credit for them

process: Plan to sustain the changes over the long haul, because trust rebuilds on a pattern, not an event. The first week of good behavior proves nothing to someone who was hurt, it is the consistency over months that does.

Make the follow-through visible without demanding credit. The changes should be observable in your behavior, but announcing look how reliable I am being turns the repair into a performance and asks them to reward you, which undercuts it.

Expect testing and setbacks. The other person may test whether the change is real, and you may slip. A slip handled honestly (naming it, correcting it immediately) can actually strengthen the repair, while a slip hidden confirms the original distrust.

Let trust return on their timeline, not yours. Pushing for the relationship to feel normal before they are ready pressures them and signals the follow-through was a means to an end, so keep the behavior steady and let them close the distance when they are ready.

steps.description: Assess honestly whether the relationship can fully recover and accept that some damage is permanent, because not every relationship returns to what it was, and a mature repair includes recognizing when the realistic outcome is a changed relationship, a reduced one, or a respectful ending rather than a full restoration.

outputs.name: acceptance-or-closure-plan
outputs.desc: How to accept the realistic outcome: a restored relationship, a changed or reduced one, or a respectful ending

process: After genuine follow-through over time, read the realistic ceiling of the recovery from their response, not from your hope. Some relationships return fully, some settle into a changed form, some reduce to civil distance, and some cannot continue.

Accept that some damage is permanent without treating that as failure. You can do the repair perfectly and still not get the relationship back, because the other person has their own agency and some injuries change a relationship for good.

Match your acceptance to the realistic outcome. If it recovered, invest in the changed relationship on its new footing. If it reduced, hold it at the level it can sustain without forcing more. If it ended, let it end with the ownership intact and without demanding absolution.

Take the durable gain regardless of outcome: you owned your part, you changed real behavior, and you learned what the damage was. That stands even if the relationship does not, and it is what you carry into every relationship that follows.
